moduleMetadata.title: Safe Browsing & Device Hygiene
moduleMetadata.description: Maintain security while navigating the web and ensure your devices are updated and protected against malware.
moduleMetadata.whyThisMatters: Your browser and devices are constantly connected to the digital world. Every day, you may visit websites, download files, install applications, open documents, connect to Wi-Fi, log into accounts, receive notifications, and update software. These everyday activities can introduce security risks when performed without enough caution.
moduleMetadata.learningOutcome: Users should be able to recognize potentially suspicious websites and maintain better device security practices.

learningObjectives: Recognize safe browsing indicators like HTTPS.
Identify signs of fake or suspicious websites.
Understand the risks of unsafe downloads and unofficial software.
Apply software and operating system updates correctly.
Implement basic device protection and malware prevention.

sections.title: Safe Browsing Practices
sections.content: Navigating the web safely requires awareness of where you are and what you are interacting with.

subsections.title: The HTTPS Lock
subsections.content: The 'HTTPS' and the padlock icon in your browser mean the connection to the site is encrypted. However, be careful—attackers can also use HTTPS on their malicious sites. It means the connection is private, but it doesn't guarantee the site is 'good'.

subsections.title: Website Awareness
subsections.content: Look for signs of low quality or suspicion: excessive pop-ups, weird domain names (e.g., 'free-movies-2026.xyz'), and requests for personal info before you've even seen the content.

sections.title: The Risk of Unsafe Downloads
sections.content: Downloading files is a high-risk activity. Only download from trusted, official sources.
bulletPoints: Avoid 'cracked' or 'premium-unlocked' software from random sites.
Be wary of 'Download' buttons that appear in advertisements.
Check file extensions—a file named 'Invoice.pdf.exe' is actually a program, not a document.

sections.title: Keeping Software Updated
sections.content: Updates are not just for new features; they often fix 'vulnerabilities' (security holes) that attackers use to gain access to your device.

subsections.title: Operating System (OS) Updates
subsections.content: Regularly update Windows, macOS, iOS, or Android.

subsections.title: Application Updates
subsections.content: Update browsers (Chrome, Firefox), Office apps, and other software.

sections.title: Malware Prevention
sections.content: Malware (Viruses, Trojans, Spyware) can steal your data or lock your computer.
tips: Don't ignore security warnings from your browser or OS.
Avoid clicking on 'You have 10 viruses!' pop-ups—those ARE the malware.

interactiveExercises.title: Website Investigation
interactiveExercises.question: You need to download a video editor. Which site is the safest choice?
options: A link sent by an unknown person in a forum.
A pop-up that says 'Your video editor is out of date, click here'.
interactiveExercises.explanation: Official sources are the most reliable way to avoid malware-infected software.

interactiveExercises.title: URL Safety Checker
interactiveExercises.instruction: Enter a URL to analyze its domain structure and risk indicators.

scenarios.title: Look-alike University Domain
scenarios.content: You see a link for university-login-example.com, but your university's real site is university.edu.
scenarios.action: Do not enter credentials. This is a look-alike domain designed to steal your login.
scenarios.lesson: Always verify the domain name in the address bar.

choices.text: Enter your credentials — the page looks identical to the real one
choices.consequence: The look-alike domain captures whatever you type. The attacker now has your username and password and can log in from their own device.

choices.text: Close the page and navigate to the university portal by typing the known address yourself
choices.consequence: You avoid the attacker-controlled page entirely. If a real login is needed, you will reach it through the official domain.

choices.text: Hover over the link, see it looks similar, and proceed
choices.consequence: Look-alike domains are designed to survive a quick glance. "university-login-example.com" is not the same as "university.edu" and will still steal credentials.

choices.text: Save your password in the browser so you do not have to type it
choices.consequence: Password managers usually refuse to auto-fill on an unrecognized domain — but if they do, you just stored your credentials in a place the attacker can now trigger to auto-submit.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Close the page and navigate to the university portal by typing the known address yourself

scenarios.title: The Virus Pop-up
scenarios.content: While browsing, a window appears: 'WARNING: Your device has 12 viruses! Install SecureFix now to clean them.'
scenarios.action: Close the window/browser tab immediately. Do not click anything inside the pop-up.
scenarios.lesson: Scareware uses fake warnings to trick you into installing real malware.

choices.text: Click "Install SecureFix" to clean the viruses
choices.consequence: The "antivirus" is the malware. Installing it gives the attacker persistent access, keylogging, and ransomware capability on your device.

choices.text: Call the support number shown in the pop-up
choices.consequence: The number routes to a scam call center that will ask for remote access to your computer and a credit card to "fix" a problem that does not exist.

choices.text: Close the browser tab (or force-quit the browser) without clicking inside the pop-up
choices.consequence: Scareware cannot scan your device — it is a web page pretending to be a scan. Closing the tab ends the attack with no installation and no data exposed.

choices.text: Restart the computer and log back in
choices.consequence: Restarting is safer than installing anything, but unnecessary — the "warning" only existed in that browser tab. You lose unsaved work for no gain.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Close the browser tab (or force-quit the browser) without clicking inside the pop-up

scenarios.title: The Update Alert
scenarios.content: You get a system notification from Windows/macOS about a security update. At the same time, a website you are on says 'Browser Update Required' with a download button.
scenarios.action: Trust the system notification. Never download 'updates' from a random website.
scenarios.lesson: Legitimate updates come through your device's built-in update tool, not a website pop-up.

choices.text: Click the website's download button — it is faster than waiting for the OS update
choices.consequence: Website-prompted "updates" are a common malware delivery channel. You are about to install an attacker-controlled executable.

choices.text: Apply only the OS-level notification and ignore the website's prompt
choices.consequence: Legitimate updates arrive through your device's built-in update mechanism. The OS notification is signed and verified; a website prompt is not.

choices.text: Download from the website, then run an antivirus scan on it
choices.consequence: Antivirus may not yet recognize a freshly released payload. Running the file at all gives it a chance to execute before the scan finishes.

choices.text: Skip both updates to avoid the hassle
choices.consequence: You leave a known vulnerability unpatched. Attackers automate exploitation of exactly these skipped updates within days of their disclosure.

scenarios.correctAnswer: Apply only the OS-level notification and ignore the website's prompt

quiz.question: What does HTTPS stand for?
quiz.explanation: The 'S' at the end indicates that the connection to the website is encrypted.

quiz.question: Does a padlock icon mean a website is 100% safe and trustworthy?
options: No, it only means the connection is encrypted.
quiz.correctAnswer: No, it only means the connection is encrypted.
quiz.explanation: Attackers can use HTTPS on malicious sites to appear legitimate and encrypt their own communications.

quiz.question: Why are software updates important for security?
options: They make the icons look better.
They fix vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit.
They give you more storage space.
quiz.correctAnswer: They fix vulnerabilities that attackers can exploit.
quiz.explanation: Security updates 'patch' holes in software that could let malware in.

quiz.question: Which file extension is most likely a suspicious program if it's supposed to be a PDF document?
quiz.explanation: The actual file extension is the one at the very end. .exe files are executable programs.

quiz.question: What should you do if a website tells you your computer is infected with viruses?
options: Call the number on the screen.
Pay the fine it asks for.
quiz.explanation: Websites cannot scan your local computer for viruses; these are fake warnings.

quiz.question: Which of these is the SAFEST place to download a new app for your phone?
options: A link from a friend's SMS.
The official Apple App Store or Google Play Store.
A random website found on Google.
quiz.correctAnswer: The official Apple App Store or Google Play Store.
quiz.explanation: Official stores vet apps for security before allowing them to be listed.

quiz.question: Browser 'Safe Browsing' warnings (red screens) should be:
options: Taken seriously and the site should be closed.
Clicked through to see what the site looks like.
quiz.correctAnswer: Taken seriously and the site should be closed.
quiz.explanation: These warnings indicate the site is known to host malware or phishing content.

quiz.question: Vulnerability refers to:
options: A weakness in a computer system that can be exploited.
A new feature in a software update.
quiz.correctAnswer: A weakness in a computer system that can be exploited.
quiz.explanation: Attackers look for vulnerabilities to gain unauthorized access.

keyTakeaways: HTTPS protects your connection but doesn't guarantee the site's intent.
Always download software from official, trusted sources.
Install security updates for your OS and apps as soon as they are available.
Never trust pop-up warnings about viruses on your device.
reflectApply: Check your computer and phone for pending updates. Are you up to date?
Think about the last three apps you downloaded. Did they come from an official store?
